title: Service Discovery & DNS 📡
description: Learn how Kubernetes DNS enables Pods to find Services by name.

slides.title: No Hard‑Coded IPs! 🚫
slides.content:
# Use names, not IPs

Instead of connecting to `10.96.0.15` (which might change if you recreate the Service), you connect to a **DNS name** that Kubernetes automatically creates:

```
<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
```

For a Service named `backend` in the `default` namespace:
```
backend.default.svc.cluster.local
```
Even shorter within the same namespace: just `backend`.

slides.title: CoreDNS Architecture 🧬
slides.content:
## The cluster’s DNS server

Kubernetes runs a DNS pod (usually **CoreDNS**) in the `kube-system` namespace. Every Pod is configured with this DNS server via `/etc/resolv.conf`.

When a Pod does a DNS lookup for a Service name, CoreDNS returns the Service’s ClusterIP.

CoreDNS also watches the Kubernetes API for new Services and Endpoints, updating its records automatically.

quizData.question: What is the full DNS name of a Service `api` in namespace `prod`?

slides.title: Testing DNS Resolution 🧪
slides.content:
## From inside a Pod

Run a temporary Pod with `busybox` or `dnsutils`:
```bash
kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup backend
```

You should see the Service’s ClusterIP and the name resolution. Use `ping` (if allowed) or `wget` to test connectivity.

slides.title: Debug DNS Example
slides.codeSnippet:
kubectl run -it --rm debug --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sh
# Inside the container:
nslookup backend.default.svc.cluster.local
wget -O- http://backend

quizData.question: What does CoreDNS return when you resolve a Service name?

options.text: The Pod IPs of the Service

quizData.explanation: Service DNS returns the ClusterIP; traffic then gets load balanced via kube‑proxy.

slides.title: Environment Variables (Legacy) 📦
slides.content:
## Another way to discover Services

Before DNS, Kubernetes injected environment variables into Pods for each Service that existed at Pod startup time. Example:
```
BACKEND_SERVICE_HOST=10.96.0.10
BACKEND_SERVICE_PORT=80
```

**Downside:** only Services that existed before the Pod started are visible. DNS is dynamic and preferred.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use headless Services for direct Pod DNS (next lesson)

If you need to resolve individual Pod IPs (e.g., for a StatefulSet), set `clusterIP: None` to get a headless Service.

quizData.question: Which Service discovery method is dynamic (works for new Services after Pod starts)?
quizData.explanation: DNS lookups are live, while env vars are only set at Pod creation.
